Photograph: Veronica Miller Australian climate and environmental reporting Bird flu ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Supported by About this content Petra Stock Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 17.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It has only been three weeks since H5 bird flu was detected on South Australia’s Limestone Coast and already encounters with sick or dead birds are becoming commonplace. Maureen Christie, who lives in the seaside town of Carpenter Rocks, has been observing and protecting birds in the region for decades. She is now witnessing many stricken and suffering. “It’s just awful,” Christie said, who helped establish the Friends of Shorebirds SE more than 20 years ago. “We expected it but, now it’s here, it’s just traumatic.” The state’s south-east is renowned for its bird life, she said, which includes resident hooded plovers and oyster catchers, along with fly-ins from other countries, such as double-banded plovers, red-necked stints, sanderlings and ruddy turnstones. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Locals have been following state government advice to “avoid, record and report”, she said. Christie said many people have been getting in touch by email and phone to relay their own sightings and reports. “Everybody’s feeling distressed, but everybody’s trying to be supportive of one another.” Since the first case in a local Australian seabird – a greater crested tern – was detected in early July, the region has seen dozens more suspected and confirmed cases, including the first confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks , a group of islets about 8km from the coastal town of Robe. “Robe has a very special and unique environment that the local community knows, uses, celebrates and cares for,” the president of Friends of Little Dip Conservation Park and Robe Coast Care, Roland Wells, said. There’s everything from migratory, coastal and inland birds, wombats, wallabies and echidnas, as well as marine mammals such as sea lions, seals and dolphins. He said people have undertaken conservation work over many decades to support shorebirds, which makes the recent arrival of bird flu “very upsetting”. The situation has escalated considerably over the past week. Council officers from Robe district council have been identifying and reporting sick and deceased birds almost daily, mainly greater crested terns and some silver gulls. Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed Read more A spokesperson for South Australia’s primary industries department said crested terns – which make up many of the bird flu cases – “commonly commingle” with other species like cormorants, gulls, grebes, ducks and other tern species. This increases the potential for transmission. “From a conservation perspective, several threatened and priority species have been identified as high risk, including fairy terns ,” the spokesperson said. “Marine mammals are also being closely monitored, with Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals among the species considered most vulnerable to potential impacts from the virus.” Wildlife carers and clinics – now required to don personal protective equipment and undertake strict cleaning and quarantine measures when dealing with other wild birds injured by cars, in dog and cat attacks or entanglement – have been calling on the state government for support. Mish Simpson, from SKER wildlife veterinary centre, said the clinic was already at capacity before bird flu. But now, more wild birds are being brought in because other vets have stopped accepting them, partly due to the additional requirements and the risk of exposure for other animals. Simpson is concerned there is not enough emphasis on slowing the spread, which would give vets, carers and the community more time to prepare. For example, she said, the dead bodies of infected birds are often being left in the environment, where they pose an infection risk to other wildlife, particularly scavengers. As the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, observed on Monday , the events rapidly unfolding in the south-east, and around Australia, are “the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife”. In Victoria , the chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said recent aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson has already shown “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”, consistent with deaths in South Australia. “Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change.” What that means for hundreds of native species and the people who care for them remains uncertain. Photograph: Lokajski/archiwum Elzbiety Moczarskiej/Elzbieta Moczarska/Fotonova Books Conversations with an Executioner: a chilling classic reveals the mind of a Nazi mass murderer Nearly 50 years after it was published, a book written by a Polish war hero, outlining his dialogue with an SS general cellmate has finally been translated into English Jo Glanville Mon 17 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 02.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n 1949, Kazimierz Moczarski, a leading member of the Polish resistance, was in his fourth year of incarceration when he was moved into a cell with two Nazis at Warsaw’s Mokotów prison. One of them was Jürgen Stroop – a war criminal and SS general who had led the infamous destruction of the Warsaw ghetto and was responsible for the murder or capture of more than 56,000 Jews. They shared the same four walls for 255 consecutive days. A celebrated figure in modern-day Poland , Moczarski was regarded as a threat to the power of the postwar communist regime in the country. Like other resistance members, he was accused of collaboration and arrested. But Moczarski, who spoke German, used his imprisonment with Stroop as an opportunity to investigate a question: what turned some Germans into mass murderers, seeking to impose their “ Ordnung ”, order, across the world? His book about the experience, Conversations with an Executioner, was published in 1977. An instant bestseller, it was performed as a play the same year, directed by Andrzej Wajda. It is finally being published in the UK this month, in its first uncensored translation into English by Sean Gasper Bye. Publisher Clare Bullock heard about the book by chance nearly 10 years ago when she was studying Polish. “In one of my lessons, we were talking about books, Polish classics. And this wonderful teacher, he said, ‘Well, there’s this one book. I don’t understand why it’s never been published here. It’s absolutely extraordinary.’” It was not until she joined Duckworth Books as editorial director in 2024 that she had the opportunity to publish it. Next year is the 50th anniversary of the book’s publication and the 120th of Moczarski’s birth. There will be events to mark the occasion in Poland. Stroop was an unrepentant fascist. He had been sentenced to death by the US military tribunal at Dachau and was awaiting trial in Poland. His cellmate Moczarski had been a member of the Home Army, the main resistance group, and had even taken part in plans to assassinate him. Yet Stroop told him his life story with little inhibition, from his rapid rise in the SS to the shocking details of the obliteration of the Warsaw ghetto in 1943. View image in fullscreen Kazimierz Moczarski in 1956. Photograph: archiwum Elzbiety Moczarskiej/Fotonova The memoir offers a remarkable insight into the genesis and mindset of a Nazi war criminal. “Remember that Stroop lived in the shadow of the gallows,” Moczarski later said in an interview, “and this situation encourages people to talk.” The third man in the cell, Gustav Schielke, had been a low-ranking SS officer, who was not fully signed up to the Nazi cause, and he joined Moczarski in cross-questioning Stroop about his activities during the war. The highly charged relationship between the three men reads like a drama: they sparred with each other, but they also shared a solidarity as prisoners, becoming anxious when one of them was taken out of the cell for interrogation. Jürgen Stroop was executed in Poland in 1952, while Moczarski was released from prison in 1956. He wrote the book while working as a journalist and assiduously factchecked Stroop’s version of events. “My father tried to talk to publishers in the late 60s, but the book was banned, totally banned,” says Elżbieta Moczarska, who was born in 1958, the only child of Moczarski and his wife Zofia. Her mother was also in the resistance and was arrested after the war as well. “Everyone obviously wanted to hear about the Nazis, but nobody wanted to have information on why a hero, somebody who was very high in the resistance, was put into the same cell [as Nazis] and was imprisoned for such a long time.” It was finally serialised in a literary magazine in the early 70s and then published as a book after Moczarski’s death, with the permission of the Communist party, in a censored edition. Elżbieta spent nearly 40 years trying to get a complete translation published in English. Moczarski allowed Stroop to condemn himself in his own words. The Nazi unashamedly relived his genocidal glory days despite his hostile audience, holding forth about his life with such candour that he is sometimes as comic as he is chilling. In one memorable scene, Stroop demonstrated how to ride a horse in the prison cell, whinnying and snorting. His repeated lascivious references to women’s breasts are almost a running gag. “I think we all talk about Hannah Arendt and the banality of evil, but this is it in one man,” says Bullock. It was not possible for Moczarski to take any notes in prison and he had to write the book from memory, so can his reports of the conversations with Stroop and Schielke be trusted as a reliable account? “My father built a kind of castle in his head,” says his daughter Elżbieta. “He could write in his head. He said once that for long-term prisoners the ability to hear is different and you learn to remember.” Moczarski said that he could replay his conversations with Stroop as if they were a tape recording. Bullock points to Solzhenitsyn’s similarly exceptional memory when imprisoned – he was able to compose and remember a poem of 7,000 lines in his head. “I think a lot of it must just have been astonishing recall backed up by serious research,” she says. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Bookmarks Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/03/feder.text: A US federal judge blocked the Trump administration on Wednesday from enforcing a new executive order limiting who qualifies for birthright citizenship.The move thwarts President Donald Trump's latest attempt to restrict the constitutional right, which comes after the US Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.US District Judge Deborah Boardman of Maryland issued a preliminary injunction following an appeal by rights groups who challenged Trump's executive order from 6 August targeting what he termed "birth tourism.""The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are 'citizens at birth'," Boardman wrote in her 35-page ruling, adding the president's August order "is almost certainly unconstitutional."Immigrant rights groups cheered the decision."When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the Supreme Court, and lost again today," said Shana Khader, Legal Director at We Are CASA, a Maryland-based group.Trump's latest executive order was aimed at those who he alleges enter the country under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth.In his first executive order on the issue, Trump said that children born to parents in the United States illegally or on temporary visas would not automatically become US citizens.Lower courts blocked that move, ruling that under the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, nearly everyone born on US soil is an American citizen. The Supreme Court agreed.The administration's attorneys argued that the request to block the order was premature and said the federal agencies tasked with enforcing it would use “appropriate measures” to do so, relying on official guidance that hasn't been issued yet.The judge rejected that argument.“No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children,” Boardman wrote.“The White House must recognise it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution,” said Khader in a prepared statement.The president's efforts to curb birthright citizenship are part of his wider campaign to limit immigration, which includes expelling millions of undocumented migrants and removing deportation protections from nationals of more than a dozen countries.
